sentences.text: Suskityrannus is a small tyrannosauroid theropod whose name means "coyote tyrant".
Known specimens have skulls measuring between 25 and 32 cm in length, while the animals stood approximately one meter tall and were three meters long.
These creatures weighed between 20 and 40 kilograms.
The skull and feet of Suskityrannus are much thinner than those of other tyrannosauroids.
Despite this slender build, the animal possessed key tyrannosauroid body plan traits, including the oldest known phylogenetic record of an arctometatarsalian foot in tyrannosauroids.
Bone ring analysis concluded that one of the specimens was approximately 3 years old.
As one of the most basal tyrannosauroid forms, Suskityrannus had a U-shaped snout and an arctometatarsalian foot.
The original fossils were discovered in 1998 by geologist Robert Denton and teenager Sterling Nesbitt during an excavation led by Doug Wolfe.
The holotype and paratype specimens are preserved in the collections of the Arizona Museum of Natural History.
Suskityrannus shows early adaptations to a combination of greater bite force and a more active running lifestyle.
In 2019, Suskityrannus was placed basally in Tyrannosauroidea, just below Timurlengia in the family tree, making it one of the few known mid-Cretaceous tyrannosauroids.
Suskityrannus hazelae lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 92 million years ago, in what is now North America.
Suskityrannus lived between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago during the Turonian stage.
The type specimen was found in the Turonian-aged Moreno Hill Formation of the Zuni Basin in western New Mexico.
The original 1998 identification of Suskityrannus as a dromaeosaurid was not based on an exhaustive examination of the animal.
Researchers suggest the initial misidentification as a dromaeosaurid was influenced by the popularity of Jurassic Park and the lack of conflict with the fossil's size, location, and age.
